main.description: A language of the Leksis dictionary, identified by its IETF (BCP 47) tag. Records prove authorship, not ownership: any user may publish a record for any tag, and the AppView treats the latest record for a tag as the current version, archiving previous ones. By convention the record key is the normalized (lowercase) tag.

tag.description: Well-formed IETF BCP 47 language tag, normalized to lowercase (e.g. "br", "br-gw").

translations.description: Names of this language in other languages. Must contain the endonym: an item whose languageID equals this record's tag, giving the language's name in itself.

grammar.description: The grammatical vocabulary this language uses, each atom bound to a label written in this language. Optional: a language with nothing declared stays fully usable, and unbound tags on its entries still render. It must be COHERENT to be indexed: every row above layer 1 may only name atoms, feature names and values this same object binds, no two rows may key the same, a named combination holds at least two atoms and must be reachable by removing one inherent feature at a time, a feature is inherent to a category XOR an axis of it, an axis names at least one value, a layout dimension names an axis that category declares, and a lexicographic label set is used nowhere in the grammatical layers. The AppView refuses a version that breaks any of these and keeps the previous one current — not because the vocabulary is wrong (a language may bind anything well-formed, minted or documented) but because the editing interface navigates these relations, so a row hanging off something undeclared can be neither reached nor repaired there. The declared maxLength of every array here is likewise enforced, not advisory.

createdAt.description: Client-declared creation time of this record version.

grammar.description: A language's declared grammatical inventory. Binding is how a language declares what it uses, so these arrays are its vocabulary: what is absent is simply not offered when authoring. Only authored rows are stored — there is no skeleton of unbound atoms, since absence already means unbound. Layer 1 declares the atoms (`pos`, `features`, `values`); layer 2 declares what they combine into (`inherent`, `bindings`); layer 3 declares what a category's forms vary over (`axes`); layer 4 declares the shape of the tables printing those cells (`layout`). They all share one object because they reference each other: unbinding an atom orphans every higher row that uses it, and one self-contained object means a single write keeps the whole cascade consistent. Two further declarations here are lexicography rather than grammar and take part in no cascade: a feature flagged `lexicographic` (register, domain, editorial usage) and the plain `abbreviations`.

pos.description: Parts of speech this language uses.

features.description: Grammatical feature names this language uses. A feature name must be bound before any of its values can be.

values.description: Feature values this language uses, each stating which feature it is an option of.

inherent.description: Which features are inherent to which category — a property of the word itself, not of one of its forms: aspect is inherent to a Slavic verb, gender to a French noun, while number varies across a noun's forms and is therefore not declared here. This is what a headword can be tagged with, and what the entry editor offers one step at a time.

bindings.description: Labels for combinations of two or more atoms — French "nf." for NOUN + Gender=Fem, where a language that prints "n. f." simply binds the two atoms separately and never adds a row here. A one-atom label belongs in `pos` or `values`, so that every fact has exactly one home. A combination must be reachable through the `inherent` declarations that build it up.

axes.description: Which features vary across a category's forms, and which values they vary over — the other half of what `inherent` declares, and together with it the coordinate system of this category's paradigm. Gender is inherent to a French noun while number varies across its forms, so number is declared here. This is what the entry editor offers when labelling another form of a word, and what `layout` arranges as a table.

layout.description: The shape of a category's inflection tables: which axis sits on which dimension, one table or several, in what order, and what is shown without asking. Axes alone underdetermine this — four axes could be one grid with nested headers or four separate tables — and where no layout is declared an entry's forms are shown as a flat list, which is the fallback this layer must never break.

abbreviations.description: Traditional dictionary abbreviations, standing for no tag at all — "udb." for "un dra bennak". They reference nothing here and nothing references them; they live in this object because a contributor opening "the labels of this language" means one shelf, and splitting a dictionary's front matter across two records would buy nothing.

layoutDeclaration.description: How one category's forms are laid out. The category is a tag and is matched the way an axis's is — the entry's own categories or any part of them — so a layout declared on {NOUN} serves an entry declared a feminine noun, and where several match, the most specific wins. A layout carries no labels and no values of its own: everything a reader sees is resolved through the rows its axes and coordinates point at.

category.description: The category whose forms are laid out: a single atom this language has bound (a part of speech, or a feature value), or a combination of them.

blocks.description: The tables and lists this category's forms are shown in, in the order they are shown. Several blocks is how a paradigm stops being rectangular: a Latin conjugation is one table per mood and tense, plus a list for the infinitive, gerund and supine that no cell of the finite grid reaches.

layoutBlock.description: One table or list of a layout. A table assigns axes to its dimensions and derives its cells from the values those axes declared — the cells are never stored, or they could drift from the axes they came from. A list names its cells explicitly, which is what prints "rosa, rosae" beside a headword and what fixes the order of the flat list of forms.

kind.description: "table" for a grid derived from axes, "list" for explicitly named cells in order.

summary.description: Show this block beside the headword rather than behind the expander — a Latin dictionary prints the genitive and expects the reader to derive the rest. When no block of a layout is marked, all of them are shown: a language that has said nothing about summarising is not asking for anything to be hidden.

fixed.description: Coordinates constant across the whole block — "Mood=Ind|Tense=Pres" for one table of a conjugation. They are part of every cell's address, and they are what the block is captioned with, so a language that named the combination gets its own label for it rather than a synthesised one. Each must be bound in `values`, but need not be an axis: pinning a constant outside the paradigm's coordinate system is a legitimate thing for a table to do.

rows.description: Feature names on the vertical dimension, outermost first — nesting is what makes a header span, and a paradigm's dimensions are not always two. Each must be an axis of this layout's category. May be empty: one axis on `columns` alone is a single-line table.

columns.description: Feature names on the horizontal dimension, outermost first. The same feature must not appear on both dimensions, or one cell would need two of its values at once.

exclude.description: Cells this paradigm does not have. A complete address removes one cell; an incomplete one removes every cell containing it, so a defective plural is one row rather than one per cell. A line or column left entirely excluded is dropped rather than printed empty — "these forms do not exist" and "nobody has entered these forms yet" must not look the same to a reader. Each coordinate must name a value of one of this block's own dimensions, since one that does not removes nothing at all.

items.description: For a list, the addresses to print, in the order they are printed. Each coordinate must be bound in `values`; unlike a table's dimensions they need not be axes, so a language can print a form it has never declared as varying.

layoutCell.description: An addressed cell. A list's item is a full address — the cell it prints — while an exclusion may be partial, and then it names a whole row, column or slice.

layoutCoord.description: One coordinate: a bare feature and value, carrying no provenance and no label. A layout is a selection from what this language has already declared, never a second place to declare it, so provenance is read back from the `values` row the pair names — which is how a cell of a minted value addresses the same tag a form authored through this language's own editor carries.

feature.description: The feature, e.g. "Case". Matched by name, as everywhere else in this record.

value.description: The value, e.g. "Gen". Several comma-separated values mean one form spanning them all ("Fem,Masc").

axisDeclaration.description: "For this category, this feature varies across its forms, over these values, in this order." The values are named rather than inherited from everything the language has bound, because a language's inventory and one category's paradigm are not the same set: a language may distinguish three genders in its adjectives while splitting the masculine of its nouns in two, personal and non-personal. Naming them also fixes the order they are shown in — the alphabetical order of an identifier is not a grammatical order. Since the category is itself a tag, an axis can be declared on a combination, which is how a paradigm stops being rectangular: declaring person an axis of a finite verb and never of an infinitive leaves the infinitive with no person cells rather than with empty ones.

category.description: The category whose forms vary: a single atom this language has bound (a part of speech, or a feature value), or a combination of them.

feature.description: Name of the varying feature, e.g. "Number". Must itself be bound in `features`; matched by name, exactly as an `inherent` declaration matches its own feature. The same feature must not be declared both inherent to a category and an axis of it — a paradigm cannot be built from a coordinate that is also a constant.

values.description: The values this category's forms range over, in the order they are shown. Each must be bound in `values` under this row's feature; matched by name, so a value minted on a Universal Dependencies feature needs no special case. Several comma-separated values in one item mean a form spanning them all ("Fem,Masc").

inherentDeclaration.description: "For this category, this feature is inherent." Both halves are variables and no category is privileged: VERB × Aspect, ADJ × Degree, ADP × Conjugation (Breton conjugates its prepositions) are as ordinary as NOUN × Gender. Since the category is itself a tag, inherence can be declared on a combination — declaring a declension inherent to {NOUN, Gender=Fem} rather than to {NOUN} is what makes the entry editor ask for the gender first. That ordering is a lexicographic judgement, and it is the language's to make.

category.description: The category the feature is inherent to: a single atom this language has bound (a part of speech, or a feature value), or a combination of them.

feature.description: Name of the inherent feature, e.g. "Gender". Must itself be bound in `features`; matched by name, as a value is matched to its feature, so a value minted on a Universal Dependencies feature needs no special case.

tag.description: The combination being named, e.g. NOUN + Gender=Fem. Two or more items: a single one is an atom, and atoms are named in `pos` and `values`.

value.description: Part-of-speech name, e.g. "NOUN". One of Universal Dependencies' 17 tags, or a name this language minted when none of them fits.

scheme.description: Provenance. Absent means the item is documented by Universal Dependencies; otherwise the BCP 47 tag of the language that minted it.

references.description: Where this binding's claim comes from. A UD item's documentation URL is derivable and is not stored; on a minted item the reference is what documents the addition, which is the condition UD's extension licence attaches to it.

feature.description: Feature name, e.g. "Gender" or the layered "Number[psor]". Universal Dependencies requires the form [A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*(\[[a-z0-9]+\])?.

scheme.description: Provenance. Absent means documented by Universal Dependencies; otherwise the BCP 47 tag of the minting language.

lexicographic.description: True when this is a lexicographic label set rather than a grammatical feature: register, domain, editorial usage ("archaic", "neologism", "by extension"). Its values are ordinary tags an entry or a sense may carry, rendering and binding exactly like any other; the flag withholds only participation in the grammatical layers, so such a feature is never inherent to a category, never an axis of one, never a layout dimension and never part of a named combination — none of those describe it. A record saying otherwise is incoherent rather than invalid: the AppView reports it and indexes it anyway.

feature.description: The feature this value is an option of, e.g. "Gender". Must itself be bound in `features`.

value.description: The value, e.g. "Fem". Universal Dependencies requires the form [A-Z0-9][A-Za-z0-9]*, so a value may begin with a digit; several comma-separated values mean the item spans them all ("Gender=Fem,Masc").

scheme.description: Provenance of the feature/value pair as a whole. Absent means documented by Universal Dependencies; otherwise the BCP 47 tag of the minting language — which is how a value minted on a UD feature is expressed ("Number=Sgv", scheme "br").

abbreviation.description: A traditional dictionary abbreviation: "udb." for "un dra bennak", "s.o." for "someone". A shallow primitive standing for no tag at all — not a feature, not a value, not an option to pick from a list. Its short form is its identity, which is why both halves are required where a label's short form is optional, and why it carries no provenance: the only possible answer would be this language's own lexicographic tradition.

short.description: The abbreviated form — the row's identity, unique within a language.

long.description: What it stands for, written out.

label.description: How this language names the bound item, for a reader of this language — a Breton binding says "anv-kadarn", never "noun".

long.description: Full form — the only required half: a lone form is always the full one.

short.description: Optional abbreviated display form; when present it is shown instead of the full form, which appears on hover.

text.description: The reference's display text (a citation, source name or note).

url.description: Optional URL the reference links to.

languageID.description: BCP 47 tag of the language this name is written in.

translation.description: The language's name written in the language identified by languageID.
